title: Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 1: when the warrior stops
excerpt: An original meaning and contextual explanation of every verse in the Gita’s opening chapter.
introHtml:
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what happened when the armies assembled at Kurukshetra. Sanjaya describes their leaders, formations and conches. Arjuna asks Krishna to position his chariot between the armies, sees his relatives and teachers, and refuses to fight them. His speech names the sin of killing family members and the consequences for family duties, varna lineages and ancestors. The chapter ends with Arjuna laying down his bow in grief.

Each Meaning renders the Sanskrit in English. Each Explanation follows the verse’s statements, terms and argument. Named traditional interpretations are distinguished where they differ. [1–3]

verses.meaningHtml: Dhritarashtra said: Sanjaya, when my sons and the sons of Pandu gathered at Kurukshetra, the field of dharma, eager to fight, what did they do?
verses.explanationHtml: Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what happened when the two armies assembled to fight. He distinguishes “my sons” from “the sons of Pandu,” although both belong to the Kuru family. Kurukshetra is called dharma-kṣetra, the field of dharma. The king’s question opens Sanjaya’s account of the confrontation.

verses.meaningHtml: Sanjaya said: Seeing the Pandava army drawn up for battle, King Duryodhana approached his teacher and spoke these words.
verses.explanationHtml: Sanjaya begins with Duryodhana’s response to the Pandava formation. After seeing the army drawn up, Duryodhana approaches his teacher Drona and speaks to him. The following verses contain his assessment of the opposing warriors and his own commanders.

verses.meaningHtml: Teacher, look at this great army of the sons of Pandu, arranged by the son of Drupada, your intelligent pupil.
verses.explanationHtml: Duryodhana tells Drona to look at the large Pandava army and points out that Drona’s pupil, Drupada’s son Dhrishtadyumna, has arranged it. His words emphasise that a warrior trained by the teacher now commands the opposing force. “Your intelligent pupil” identifies both Dhrishtadyumna’s training and his ability.

verses.meaningHtml: Here are heroes, great bowmen equal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna: Yuyudhana, Virata and the great chariot-warrior Drupada.
verses.explanationHtml: The opposing warriors are praised as heroes and great bowmen. Bhima and Arjuna provide the comparison for their strength in battle. Duryodhana names Yuyudhana, Virata and Drupada as examples; mahāratha, applied to Drupada, denotes a great chariot-warrior.

verses.meaningHtml: There are Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the powerful king of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja and Shaibya, an outstanding man.
verses.explanationHtml: Duryodhana continues naming the Pandava allies: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the king of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja and Shaibya. The king of Kashi is described as powerful, and Shaibya as an outstanding man. These names continue the account of the opposing army’s prominent fighters.

verses.meaningHtml: There are the brave Yudhamanyu, the vigorous Uttamaujas, Subhadra’s son and the sons of Draupadi; all are great chariot-warriors.
verses.explanationHtml: The list adds Yudhamanyu, Uttamaujas, Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra, and Draupadi’s sons. Yudhamanyu is called brave and Uttamaujas vigorous. All those named in the verse are described as great chariot-warriors. Subhadra’s and Draupadi’s sons bring the younger Pandava generation into the list.

verses.meaningHtml: Know also the distinguished men on our side, foremost among the twice-born. For your information, I will name the leaders of my army.
verses.explanationHtml: Having named leading warriors on the Pandava side, Duryodhana turns to his own army. He tells Drona that he will identify its commanders. “Foremost among the twice-born” addresses Drona as a Brahmin; the second birth refers to religious initiation.

verses.meaningHtml: There are yourself, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa who is victorious in battle, Ashvatthama, Vikarna and the son of Somadatta.
verses.explanationHtml: Duryodhana names Drona, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashvatthama, Vikarna and Somadatta’s son. “Yourself” addresses Drona, the teacher listening to the speech. The epithet attached to Kripa praises his victory in battle. Together these names identify the leading strength of Duryodhana’s army.

verses.meaningHtml: Many other heroes are ready to give their lives for my sake. They carry different weapons and are all skilled in battle.
verses.explanationHtml: Duryodhana says that many further heroes have committed their lives to his cause. Their readiness to die, variety of weapons and knowledge of warfare complete his description of the army’s strength. The phrase “for my sake” identifies him as the person for whom they are prepared to fight.

verses.meaningHtml: Our force, protected by Bhishma, is insufficient; their force, protected by Bhima, is sufficient.
verses.explanationHtml:
The word aparyāptam supports an important difference in interpretation. Read as “insufficient,” Duryodhana’s statement reveals anxiety despite his impressive list of allies. Read as “unlimited,” it becomes a boast that his side’s strength exceeds the more limited opposing force.

Traditional commentators preserve this disagreement: Shridhara reads the force as unable to meet the opponent, while Baladeva reads it as immeasurable. The meaning above follows the first reading. Both keep the same Sanskrit before the reader; the difference concerns what Duryodhana is communicating at this point. His next instruction—to protect Bhishma—can be considered alongside either interpretation. [2, 3]

verses.meaningHtml: All of you, stationed in your assigned positions at the approaches, must protect Bhishma in particular.
verses.explanationHtml: Duryodhana orders the warriors to remain at their assigned approaches and protect Bhishma in particular. The instruction follows his comparison of the two forces in 1.10. Bhishma’s protection is to be a shared task for the commanders stationed throughout the formation.

verses.meaningHtml: Then the valiant elder of the Kurus, the grandsire Bhishma, roared like a lion and blew his conch, bringing joy to Duryodhana.
verses.explanationHtml: Bhishma, the elder of the Kurus, responds by blowing his conch. His loud sound is compared to a lion’s roar, and Sanjaya states that it delights Duryodhana. The account now moves from the commander’s speech to the sounds signalling readiness for battle.

verses.meaningHtml: Conches, kettledrums, smaller drums and horns then sounded together, producing a tremendous uproar.
verses.explanationHtml: After Bhishma’s conch, the instruments of the army sound together. The verse names conches, drums and horns, then describes the combined sound as a tremendous uproar. The single signal of the previous verse is followed by the army’s collective response.

verses.meaningHtml: Then Madhava and the son of Pandu, seated in a great chariot drawn by white horses, blew their divine conches.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna and Arjuna answer from their great chariot drawn by white horses. “Madhava” names Krishna, and “the son of Pandu” identifies Arjuna. Their conches are called divine. This begins the account of the conches sounded on the Pandava side.

verses.meaningHtml: Hrishikesha blew Panchajanya, Dhananjaya blew Devadatta, and mighty Bhima, known as Vrikodara, blew the great conch Paundra.
verses.explanationHtml: The verse names each conch and its owner. Krishna, called Hrishikesha, blows Panchajanya; Arjuna, called Dhananjaya, blows Devadatta; Bhima, called Vrikodara, blows Paundra. Bhima’s great strength and the size of his conch are emphasised. The different epithets identify these same three warriors.

verses.meaningHtml: King Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, blew Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughosha and Manipushpaka.
verses.explanationHtml: Yudhishthira blows Anantavijaya, Nakula blows Sughosha, and Sahadeva blows Manipushpaka. Yudhishthira is identified as king and son of Kunti. With Bhima and Arjuna named in the preceding verse, all five Pandava brothers now have their conches identified.

verses.meaningHtml: The great archer, the king of Kashi, the great chariot-warrior Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata and undefeated Satyaki also sounded their conches.
verses.explanationHtml: The king of Kashi, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata and Satyaki join the sounding of conches. The descriptions praise their skill and strength: the king of Kashi is a great archer, Shikhandi a great chariot-warrior, and Satyaki undefeated. The list continues into the next verse.

verses.meaningHtml: Drupada, the sons of Draupadi and the mighty-armed son of Subhadra each blew their conches, O lord of the earth.
verses.explanationHtml: Drupada, Draupadi’s sons and Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra, each sound their conches. “Lord of the earth” is Sanjaya’s address to Dhritarashtra, who is hearing the account. The verse completes the list of the Pandava warriors taking part in this response.

verses.meaningHtml: That tremendous sound echoed through sky and earth and tore at the hearts of Dhritarashtra’s people.
verses.explanationHtml: The combined sound fills the earth and sky and strikes fear into Dhritarashtra’s people. “Tore at the hearts” describes its effect on their courage. The Pandava conches are thus presented as shaking the opposing army before the fighting develops.

verses.meaningHtml: Then the son of Pandu, whose banner bore the monkey emblem, saw Dhritarashtra’s people drawn up and raised his bow as the clash of weapons was beginning.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna sees Dhritarashtra’s warriors standing in battle formation and raises his bow. His banner bears the monkey emblem. Sanjaya places this action at the beginning of the clash of weapons; Arjuna is still preparing to fight when he makes the request that follows.

verses.meaningHtml: O king, Arjuna then spoke to Hrishikesha: Achyuta, place my chariot between the two armies.
verses.explanationHtml: Sanjaya addresses Dhritarashtra as “king,” then introduces Arjuna’s speech. Arjuna asks Krishna to place the chariot between the two armies. Hrishikesha and Achyuta are names of Krishna. The speaker transition separates Sanjaya’s address to the king from Arjuna’s request to his charioteer.

verses.meaningHtml: Let me look at those who stand here wanting to fight, and see with whom I must contend in this undertaking of battle.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna gives the purpose of his request: he wants to inspect the warriors who have come to fight and identify those he must oppose. The chariot’s position between the armies will let him see both formations before entering the battle. His request continues into 1.23.

verses.meaningHtml: I want to see those who have gathered here to fight, wishing to please the ill-minded son of Dhritarashtra in this battle.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna describes the opposing warriors as men gathered to please Duryodhana, the son of Dhritarashtra. He calls Duryodhana ill-minded and asks to see those who support him. This is Arjuna’s assessment of the enemy at the point when he still intends to fight.

verses.meaningHtml: Sanjaya said: Addressed in this way by Gudakesha, Hrishikesha placed the excellent chariot between the two armies, O descendant of Bharata.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna carries out Arjuna’s request and places the chariot between the armies. Sanjaya addresses Dhritarashtra as a descendant of Bharata while reporting the movement. The following verse identifies the warriors before whom Krishna brings the chariot to a halt.

verses.meaningHtml: In front of Bhishma, Drona and the other rulers, Krishna said: Partha, look at these Kurus gathered here.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna stops before Bhishma, Drona and the other rulers, then tells Arjuna to look at the assembled Kurus. The name “Kurus” identifies the shared lineage of the opposing relatives. Bhishma and Drona, Arjuna’s elder and teacher, are directly before him as he surveys the armies.

verses.meaningHtml: There Partha saw fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends standing before him.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna sees relatives of several generations, along with teachers and friends. “Fathers” includes men of his father’s generation; Pandu, his own father, has already died. The list identifies those on the field through their relationships to Arjuna, beginning the change from inspecting enemies to recognising his own people.

verses.meaningHtml: He also saw fathers-in-law and well-wishers in both armies. The son of Kunti looked over all those relatives assembled there.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna also recognises fathers-in-law and well-wishers in both armies. His relatives and connections are present on both sides of the battle. The verse completes the survey begun in 1.26, after which Sanjaya describes Arjuna’s compassion and grief.

verses.meaningHtml: Overcome by deep compassion and sinking into sorrow, Arjuna said: Krishna, seeing my own people standing here eager to fight—
verses.explanationHtml: Sanjaya says that Arjuna is overcome by compassion and sorrow at the sight of his relatives. Arjuna then begins speaking to Krishna about seeing his own people eager for battle. His sentence continues in 1.29, where he describes the bodily effects of his distress.

verses.meaningHtml: My limbs are failing, my mouth is drying up, my body is trembling and my hair is standing on end.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna names four bodily symptoms: weakness in his limbs, dryness of the mouth, trembling and his hair standing on end. These follow from seeing his relatives assembled for battle. The next verse continues his account of the condition that prevents him from standing ready to fight.

verses.meaningHtml: Gandiva slips from my hand, my skin burns, I cannot stand steady, and my mind seems to reel.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that Gandiva, his bow, slips from his hand. He feels burning in his skin, cannot remain steady and experiences his mind as reeling. His description combines loss of control over his weapon, bodily distress and mental confusion. It continues the symptoms listed in 1.29.

verses.meaningHtml: I see adverse signs, Keshava, and I see no good coming from killing my own people in battle.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna reports adverse signs and declares that killing his relatives will bring no good. Keshava is his address to Krishna. His speech now moves from bodily distress to reasons for refusing battle, beginning with his judgement about the consequences of killing his own people.

verses.meaningHtml: I do not desire victory, Krishna, nor kingship nor its pleasures. What use are a kingdom, enjoyments or even life to us, Govinda?
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna rejects the usual rewards of victory: kingship, enjoyment and pleasure. He asks what use a kingdom, its enjoyments or even life would have. The following verses explain his reason: the relatives for whose sake these rewards were desired are themselves standing in the battle.

verses.meaningHtml: Those for whose sake we wanted a kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures are standing here in battle, having put their lives and possessions at risk.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that the people for whom he and his brothers wanted kingship and enjoyment have put their lives and possessions at stake. Victory would require fighting these same people. This answers the question of 1.32 by connecting the value of the kingdom with the relatives present on the field.

verses.meaningHtml: Teachers, fathers, sons and grandfathers; maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law and other relatives are here.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna specifies the relatives and teachers whose presence troubles him. They include elders, descendants and relations by marriage. The list continues his explanation of why kingship and its pleasures no longer attract him: obtaining them would involve killing people with whom he expected to share them.

verses.meaningHtml: Madhusudana, I do not wish to kill these people, even if they kill me—not even for sovereignty over the three worlds, much less for this earth.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says he will not kill these relatives and teachers, even if they kill him. He rejects even sovereignty over the three worlds as a reward for doing so, and therefore rejects the smaller reward of ruling the earth. The comparison expresses the extent of his refusal.

verses.meaningHtml: What joy could come to us from killing Dhritarashtra’s sons, Janardana? Sin would fall upon us if we killed these aggressors.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna calls Dhritarashtra’s sons aggressors but says that killing them would bring sin upon his own side. He asks what pleasure could follow from their deaths. The verse holds both descriptions together: the men are aggressors, and they are relatives whose killing Arjuna regards as sinful.

verses.meaningHtml: Therefore we should not kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, our own relatives. How could we be happy after killing our own people, Madhava?
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna concludes that they should not kill Dhritarashtra’s sons because those sons are their own relatives. He again asks how killing one’s own people could produce happiness. The conclusion follows his claim in 1.36 that killing these aggressors would bring sin rather than joy.

verses.meaningHtml: Even if these people, their minds overcome by greed, do not see the wrong in destroying a family or the sin of betraying friends—
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that greed has blinded the opposing side to the wrong of destroying a family and betraying friends. His sentence continues in the next verse. He distinguishes their failure to see these sins from his own side’s awareness of what destroying the family would entail.

verses.meaningHtml: Why should we not know to turn away from this sin, Janardana, when we clearly see the harm caused by destroying a family?
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna asks why those who recognise the harm of destroying a family should fail to turn away from that sin. His argument rests on the difference stated in 1.38: the opponents are blinded by greed, while he and his companions can see the consequences. He then describes those consequences in 1.40–44.

verses.meaningHtml: When a family is destroyed, its longstanding family duties and traditions perish. When that dharma is lost, adharma overtakes the whole family.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that destroying a family destroys its longstanding kula-dharma: its inherited duties, rites and traditions. Once that dharma disappears, adharma overtakes the family. This begins his sequence of consequences connecting the deaths in battle with the corruption of the family, intermixture of varnas and punishment in hell.

verses.meaningHtml: When adharma prevails, Krishna, the women of the family become corrupted; and when that happens, descendant of Vrishni, intermixture of varnas arises.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna gives the next links in the sequence: when adharma prevails, the women of the family become corrupted; from their corruption comes varṇa-saṅkara, intermixture of varnas. His argument connects the preservation of family dharma with women’s conduct and the continuation of distinct varna lineages. The following verse states the consequences for the family and its ancestors.

verses.meaningHtml: Such intermixture brings hell to those who destroy a family and to the family itself. Their ancestors also fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that intermixture of varnas brings hell upon the destroyers of the family and upon the family itself. The ancestors also fall because the offerings of rice-balls and water cease. The loss of descendants maintaining these rites therefore affects the dead as well as those living after the battle.

verses.meaningHtml: Through these faults of those who destroy families, faults that cause intermixture of varnas, the longstanding duties of social groups and families are uprooted.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that the faults of those who destroy families produce intermixture of varnas and uproot enduring duties. Jāti-dharma refers to the duties of social groups, and kula-dharma to family duties. His argument links killing the family’s members with the destruction of the inherited social and ritual order.

verses.meaningHtml: Janardana, we have heard that people whose family duties have been destroyed face an indefinite stay in hell.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna appeals to what he has heard through tradition: those whose family duties have been destroyed dwell in hell. This edition reads aniyatam, rendered here as “indefinite,” for the duration of that stay. The threatened punishment completes his account of the consequences of destroying the family.

verses.meaningHtml: Alas, we have resolved to commit a great sin: out of greed for the pleasures of kingship, we are prepared to kill our own people.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna now calls his own side’s intended action a great sin. He says that greed for the pleasures of kingship has made them ready to kill their relatives. The accusation of greed that he applied to the opponents in 1.38 is here applied to “we,” including himself.

verses.meaningHtml: If Dhritarashtra’s armed sons were to kill me in battle while I remained unarmed and offered no resistance, that would be better for me.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says it would be better for him to be killed while unarmed and unresisting than to fight his relatives. Dhritarashtra’s sons would remain armed and would do the killing. This carries his refusal to its strongest statement: he prefers suffering death to carrying out the battle himself.

verses.meaningHtml: Sanjaya said: Having spoken in this way, Arjuna sat down in the chariot on the battlefield. He let fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by sorrow.
verses.explanationHtml: Sanjaya resumes the narration after Arjuna’s speech. Arjuna sits down in the chariot and lets fall his bow and arrows, overwhelmed by sorrow. His refusal to fight is now expressed through his actions. Krishna’s reply begins in Chapter 2, with Arjuna still in this condition.
